title: Filtration and centrifuges
ends: Your cakes will come out dry.

steps.q: Constant-pressure filter, cloth ignored. How long to filter twice the volume?
steps.title: Growing cake
steps.summary: During constant-pressure filtration the cake thickens and its resistance grows with the volume filtered. Ignoring cloth resistance, filtration time goes with volume squared, so twice the volume takes about four times as long, and the end of each batch is the slowest. Two thinner loads can be quicker than one thick one.

steps.q: The cake is soft and compressible. You double the filter pressure. What happens to the rate?
steps.title: Squashed cake
steps.summary: For a hard, incompressible cake the filtration rate rises roughly in proportion to pressure. A soft, compressible cake squashes as pressure rises, closing its pores, so the rate rises less than in proportion and can barely change, and very high pressure can blind the cloth. Better fixes are larger crystals or a thinner cake; filter aid suits only waste solids such as carbon, since it stays in the cake.

steps.q: The cake cracks just before washing. What happens to the wash?
steps.title: Cracked cake
steps.summary: A cake cracks if it is sucked or blown too dry or shrinks as it drains. Wash liquid then channels down the cracks and misses most of the cake, leaving mother liquor and impurities behind. Keep the cake wet until washing, smooth the cracks, or reslurry wash it.

steps.q: A centrifuge basket of half a metre radius spins at 1000 rpm. Roughly what g-force?
steps.title: G-force
steps.summary: Centrifugal force in g is ω²r ÷ g. At 1000 rpm, ω = 2π × 1000 ÷ 60 ≈ 105 rad/s, so with a 0.5 m radius G ≈ 105² × 0.5 ÷ 9.81 ≈ 560 g. At the same speed a larger basket gives more g, which squeezes more liquid from the cake.

draw: bigger basket, same rpm → more g

steps.q: You spin longer, but the cake's LOD stops falling after a few minutes. Why?
steps.title: Spin limit
steps.summary: Free liquid between crystals spins out quickly, so LOD falls fast at first. The liquid left is held in fine pores and on crystal surfaces by capillary forces, and extra spin time barely moves it. Higher g, larger crystals or a final wash with a low-viscosity, low-surface-tension solvent help more. Set the spin time where the LOD curve flattens.

steps.q: Before spinning a cake wet with toluene, what must be done?
steps.title: Inert first
steps.summary: A centrifuge spinning a solvent-wet cake is full of flammable vapour, and static from the cake or bags can ignite it. Purge with nitrogen before spinning and keep the purge on, with an oxygen analyser interlocked to block start-up and stop feeding if oxygen is above the limit, set safely below the solvent's limiting oxygen concentration (often an alarm near 5 % and a trip near 8 %, lower for some solvents). Earth the machine and use conductive bags.

opts.t: Open the lid to let vapour out

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: filters and centrifuges, where batches go to get squeezed. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now try your own filtration numbers in the filtration calculator.

q1.text: Question 1. Constant-pressure filter, cloth ignored. How long to filter twice the volume?

q1-r0.text: Twice? The cake keeps getting thicker as you go.

q1-r1.text: 4 times! The growing cake slows you down.

q1-r2.text: Same time? The cake would like to disagree.

q1-r3.text: Too much. It goes with volume squared, not cubed.

q1-b0.text: As you filter, the cake gets thicker, and the thicker cake resists flow more.

q1-b1.text: At constant pressure, the filtration time goes with the volume squared.

q1-b2.text: Twice the volume means four times the time. The last part of the batch is always the slowest.

q1-b3.text: That's why thick cakes are slow. Sometimes two thinner loads are quicker than one thick one.

q2.text: Question 2. The cake is soft and compressible. You double the filter pressure. What happens to the rate?

q2-r0.text: Only for a hard, incompressible cake. Yours squashes.

q2-r1.text: Yes! The cake squashes and closes up.

q2-r2.text: 4 times? Pressure isn't that generous, even on hard cakes.

q2-r3.text: It doesn't stop. It just doesn't help as much as you hoped.

q2-b0.text: For a hard, gritty cake, flow goes up roughly in step with pressure.

q2-b1.text: A soft cake squashes under pressure. Its pores close, so its resistance goes up.

q2-b2.text: Push harder, and you can even pack it tight enough to blind the cloth.

q2-b3.text: Better fixes: bigger crystals from the crystalliser, a thinner cake, or a filter aid where the solids are waste, like carbon.

q3.text: Question 3. The cake cracks just before washing. What happens to the wash?

q3-r0.text: Better? The wash takes the easy way out through the cracks.

q3-r1.text: Correct! Channelling. The cake stays dirty.

q3-r2.text: Cracks change everything. Liquid always takes the easy path.

q3-r3.text: It flows all right. Just in the wrong place.

q3-b0.text: A cake cracks when it's sucked or blown too dry, or shrinks as it drains.

q3-b1.text: Wash liquid takes the easy way, straight down the cracks. Most of the cake never sees it.

q3-b2.text: The mother liquor stays in the cake, and so do the impurities.

q3-b3.text: Keep the cake wet before washing, or smooth the cracks, or reslurry wash it.

q4.text: Question 4. A centrifuge basket of half a metre radius spins at 1000 rpm. Roughly what g-force?

q4-r0.text: Ten times too little. Square omega, then times the radius.

q4-r2.text: rpm and g-force aren't the same number. Do the maths.

q4-r3.text: Ten times too much. Check the radius.

q4-b0.text: G-force is omega squared times radius, divided by g.

q4-b1.text: 1000 rpm is about 105 radians per second. Squared, that's about 11 thousand.

q4-b2.text: Times half a metre, divided by 9.81. About 560 times gravity.

q4-b3.text: The same speed on a bigger basket gives more g. And more g squeezes more liquid out of the cake.

q5.text: Question 5. You spin longer, but the cake's LOD stops falling after a few minutes. Why?

q5-r0.text: It's working fine. The cake is just holding on.

q5-r1.text: Yes! Capillary liquid. More time won't shift it.

q5-r2.text: It didn't get wetter. It just stopped getting drier.

q5-r3.text: Check the speed if you like. That's not it.

q5-b0.text: Early on, free liquid between the crystals spins out fast.

q5-b1.text: What's left is held in the fine pores and on the crystal surface, by capillary forces.

q5-b2.text: More spin time barely helps. Higher g, bigger crystals, or a final wash with a thin, low-surface-tension solvent help more.

q5-b3.text: So set the spin time where the curve flattens, not longer.

q6.text: Question 6. Before spinning a cake wet with toluene, what must be done?

q6-r0.text: Correct! Spinning basket plus solvent vapour: keep the oxygen out.

q6-r1.text: Open the lid?! That lets air in. Exactly wrong.

q6-r2.text: A few litres of toluene can fill the casing with flammable vapour. Plenty for a flash fire.

q6-r3.text: Heat? You'd just make more vapour.

q6-b0.text: A spinning basket full of solvent vapour is a fire waiting for a spark. Static from the cake or the bag can give one.

q6-b1.text: So purge with nitrogen first, and keep it on while spinning.

q6-b2.text: Check the oxygen with an analyser. The interlock must stop the machine starting, and stop feeding, if oxygen is above the limit. Set it safely below the solvent's limiting oxygen value: often an alarm near 5 percent and a trip near 8, lower for some solvents.

q6-b3.text: Earth the machine and use conductive bags. Then check the numbers in the filtration calculator on pharmacheme dot in.
